![][image1]

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is used by devices to find the MAC address of another device on the same network using its IP address. The problem with ARP is that it has no verification mechanism — any device can send an ARP reply and others will trust it without question.

In this simulation, three devices are connected to a switch — PC-A as the victim (192.168.1.10), PC-C as the gateway (192.168.1.1), and PC-B as the attacker (192.168.1.20). Under normal conditions, when PC-A wants to reach the gateway, it sends an ARP request and PC-C responds with its real MAC address, which PC-A stores in its ARP cache.

The attack begins when PC-B sends a fake ARP reply to PC-A, claiming that the gateway IP (192.168.1.1) belongs to PC-B's MAC address. Since ARP has no way to verify this, PC-A accepts the reply and overwrites the legitimate entry in its ARP cache with the attacker's MAC address.

From this point onwards, any traffic PC-A sends to the gateway actually goes to PC-B instead. This is called a Man-in-the-Middle attack — the attacker sits between the victim and the gateway, able to read or manipulate all passing traffic without either side knowing.

The switch plays no role in stopping this because it only forwards frames based on MAC addresses and does not inspect ARP content. The gateway PC-C is also completely unaware since the attack targets only PC-A's cache.
